'''''Vriesea''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the [[botany|botanical]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Bromeliaceae]], subfamily [[Tillandsioideae]]. The genus is named after the [[Netherlands|Dutch]] [[botanist]] and [[physician]] [[Willem Hendrik de Vriese]] (1806–1862).<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://bsi.org/brom_info/genera.html |title=Bromeliad Society International - Genera Etymology |access-date=2007-02-22 |archive-date=2007-02-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070203011214/http://www.bsi.org/brom_info/genera.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Its species are widespread over [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], [[South America]] and the [[West Indies]].<ref name=j>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=271642 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref>

The genus includes many "tank bromeliads", which store water in a reservoir (a "[[Water tank|tank]]") formed by their tightly overlapping [[leaf]] bases. Containing some of the largest bromeliad species, these tropical plants hold a wide variety of [[insect]] fauna. In the wild, some frog species go through their whole life cycle in these bromeliad tanks.{{cn|date=August 2025}} This genus is closely related to ''[[Guzmania]]''. Both ''Guzmania'' and ''Vriesea'' have dry capsules that split open to release parachute like seeds similar to dandelions (''[[Taraxacum]]'' sp.){{cn|date=August 2025}}{{clarify|date=August 2025|reason=Dandelions don't have their seeds in dry capsules; a better comparison is needed}}. Most ''Vriesea'' are [[epiphytes]] and grow on trees. Their roots function mainly as holdfasts with a more minor role in nutrient uptake. Nutrients are predominantly absorbed from the reservoirs made by the rosette of leaves.
